bp: The ordinary object in this paper is not a single leaked address or phone number. It is a marketplace where private facts about people are turned into products that can be requested, packaged, advertised, paid for, and delivered. Doxing becomes more damaging when it stops depending on one angry person doing manual digging and becomes a service that many customers can use on demand. The paper studies that shift in Chinese cyberspace, where the abstract says Doxing-as-a-Service has grown into a commercial model for retrieving, organizing, and trading personal data. The web safety problem is therefore partly economic and partly social: lowered access costs let more people expose identities, while repeated advertising and group spaces help the market keep finding buyers. The paper serves defenders by mapping the ecosystem itself, using Telegram messages and subscriber links to reveal how providers, operators, and end users fit together.
wh: The hard part is that a doxing market is not one visible website with a checkout page and a clean customer list. It is an underground service ecosystem whose participants have reasons to hide, split roles, move across channels, and build trust without legal enforcement. A defender who only counts leaked records misses the machinery that makes the harm repeatable. The abstract says the ecosystem includes 100 major Telegram channels, 25,972 messages, and 13.22 million subscriber links, so the evidence is spread across text, channels, and relationships among subscribers. Another difficulty is that the same spaces can support several functions at once: advertising services, matching users with operators, exposing identities at scale, arranging crypto-based payments, and even mitigating fraud inside the illegal market. The central tension is that the market is harmful, but it has enough organization to behave like a resilient service industry rather than a random pile of bad posts.
naive: A smart beginner might search for doxing keywords, count how many posts expose personal information, and treat every active channel as the same kind of offender. That would catch some surface harm, but it would not explain how the business keeps running. It would miss the supply chain: data providers feed operators, operators package services, and end users create demand. It would also miss the way user groups help with real-time matching and community fraud mitigation. A second naive idea is to study only the content of posts. The paper's subscriber-link evidence matters because channels and users form a relationship map; who gathers around whom is part of the market's structure, not just background detail.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat online doxing as an ecosystem with roles, service categories, transactions, and social coordination, then measure that ecosystem from platform traces. Instead of beginning with the leaked person, it begins with the machinery that makes leaking available as a service. The authors collect messages and subscriber links from major Telegram channels, then use those traces to describe organization, operations, and user engagement. The concrete finding in the abstract is a three-tier supply chain: data providers, service operators, and end users. Operators maintain businesses through six service categories, persistent advertising, and cryptocurrency payments. Users do more than passively consume; they interact in specialized group spaces that match demand to services, enable large-scale identity exposure, and help the community reduce fraud among market participants. The core idea is measurement as demystification: make the hidden market legible by separating roles and flows.
mech: The mechanism starts with two kinds of raw evidence named in the abstract. The first is message content from Telegram channels: 25,972 messages that can show what is being advertised, requested, promised, priced, or coordinated. The second is a large relationship record: 13.22 million subscriber links from 100 major channels, which shows how attention and participation are distributed across the ecosystem. The paper then turns these traces into a map of operations. Messages are read as evidence of service categories, advertising behavior, payments, and group practices. Subscriber links are read as evidence of engagement and organization, because a channel with overlapping or specialized subscribers is not just a text feed; it is a gathering point in a market. From this evidence, the authors identify the roles in the supply chain. Data providers are the upstream source of personal information. Service operators are the middle layer that organizes, advertises, sells, and delivers doxing products. End users are the demand side, requesting or consuming identity exposure. The output is not a detector that labels one account as bad. It is a structured account of how Doxing-as-a-Service operates: which roles exist, what services are offered, how payments are supported, how users find matches in real time, and how the market tries to protect itself from fraud.
math: The main mathematical ideas are counting, categorizing, and network measurement. Counting is the simplest but necessary move: repeated messages and subscriber links turn scattered observations into evidence about scale, persistence, and engagement. Categorizing means putting messages or operations into service types so that the market is not described as one vague activity. A category is a boundary: posts inside it are treated as serving the same function, such as advertising or a service offering, while posts outside it are kept separate. Network measurement is the deeper idea. A network is a map made of places and roads; here the places are channels and subscribers, and a link records that a subscriber belongs to or follows a channel. The map matters because markets are sustained by relationships, not just by isolated text. If many users gather around specialized group spaces, those spaces can match buyers and sellers faster and help members judge which counterparties are reliable. There is also a supply-chain model, which is a directed way of thinking about flow: personal data moves from providers to operators to end users, while money and demand move back through the system. The tradeoff is visibility versus inference. The traces reveal organization, but the abstract does not say they expose every private transaction or hidden participant.
dots: This paper sits at the crossing of privacy, cybersecurity threat analysis, fraud and anomaly detection, and social-network measurement. It belongs near privacy and federated-security work because the harm begins when personal information crosses a boundary without consent, but this paper studies the attacker-side economy rather than a protective mechanism. It connects to fraud and anomaly studies because the ecosystem includes specialized group spaces for community-driven fraud mitigation; even illegal markets face trust problems when anonymous participants can cheat each other. It also connects to social-network and influence papers because the evidence is relational: channels, subscribers, and group spaces form the infrastructure through which services are advertised and matched. Unlike a fake-media paper that asks whether a post is true, this work asks how a market makes repeated harm easy. Unlike a graph-learning paper that predicts labels, it uses a graph-like view to understand organization, engagement, and resilience in an underground web ecosystem.
ww: The approach works better than counting leaked items because the thing that needs explaining is repeatability. A one-off leak can be described by the exposed facts. A service market must be described by roles, channels, payments, advertising, matching, and trust repair. The three-tier supply-chain view helps because it separates different kinds of work that a single surface label, doxer, would collapse. Providers solve the supply problem by obtaining personal data. Operators solve the product and distribution problem by organizing services, advertising them persistently, and accepting crypto-based payments. End users solve the demand problem by bringing requests and attention into group spaces. The message evidence can show what is offered and how it is promoted, while subscriber-link evidence can show where people gather and how large the engagement structure is. The mechanism should improve understanding because it follows the market's own operating parts. It explains not only that doxing happens, but how barriers fall when a customer can enter a channel, find an operator, pay, and rely on community signals.
po: The payoff is a first systematic picture of the Chinese Doxing-as-a-Service ecosystem, grounded in a concrete dataset rather than anecdotes. The paper identifies a three-tier supply chain, six major service categories, persistent advertising, crypto-based payments, and user spaces that support matching, identity exposure, and fraud mitigation. That gives web safety researchers and platform defenders a more useful target than individual posts alone. If the market is organized through channels, roles, and payments, then interventions can be reasoned about at those pressure points: reducing discovery, disrupting operators, monitoring service advertising, or understanding how trust is built inside harmful markets.
limits: The abstract supports ecosystem measurement, not a complete census of all Chinese doxing activity. The dataset comes from 100 major Telegram channels, so it may miss smaller, private, deleted, migrated, or non-Telegram spaces. Subscriber links show association with channels, not necessarily purchase, intent, or successful doxing. Message analysis can reveal advertised services and visible coordination, but hidden negotiations and off-platform payments may remain unseen. The abstract also does not prove which interventions would work, whether the same structure appears in other countries, or how accurately every role can be assigned from traces alone.
